red.focus: Explain why economic success is not the whole purpose of law
red.summary: Laws can influence prosperity and cooperation, but they also protect rights and dignity. Learn why a profitable outcome is not automatically a just outcome.
checklist: I can distinguish wealth from legal legitimacy
I can identify people helped and harmed by a rule
I can explain why rights can limit efficient choices

sections.title: Useful Rules Can Still Be Unfair
sections.body_md: A city could save money by denying every application for emergency shelter without review. Its budget might improve, but the measure could violate legal duties and place vulnerable people in danger. Economic cost is important, yet it does not alone establish what officials may lawfully do. A student should separate financial effects from rights, procedures and obligations. The purpose of law includes protecting people against wrongful exercises of power, not merely producing high aggregate savings.

The purpose of law includes protecting people against wrongful exercises of power, not merely producing high aggregate savings.

sections.title: People Are Not Abstract Units
sections.body_md: A policy may improve average income while leaving a minority exposed to greater injury. Averages describe groups but can hide unequal burdens. Good evaluation identifies whose lives change, what alternatives exist and whether protected rights are respected. Economic analysis becomes more valuable when it makes these differences visible rather than declaring that the majority's gain settles every issue. Justice requires reasons for how burdens are allocated.

sections.title: Why Study Economics at All?
sections.body_md: Because lawyers must understand how people and institutions respond to rules. A sanction that is never enforced may not prevent harm, while a confusing procedure may keep eligible people from receiving benefits. Economics supplies tools for examining incentives, costs and outcomes. Legal legitimacy supplies another question: is the chosen action authorized, fair and accountable? Masterful legal education uses both rather than replacing one with the other.

yellow.focus: Distinguish Pareto and Kaldor-Hicks claims from legal justice
yellow.summary: Learn the basic welfare concepts used to evaluate policy and their limitations. Recognize why an economic improvement does not necessarily provide consent, compensation or equal protection.
checklist: I can explain a Pareto improvement
I can distinguish welfare criteria from binding legal standards

sections.title: A Pareto Improvement Has a Narrow Definition
sections.body_md: A change is Pareto-improving when at least one person benefits and no one is made worse off under the chosen evaluation. Such changes are attractive but often hard to find in contested public policy. A new rail link may benefit many commuters while imposing noise on some homes. Calling it Pareto-improving without considering those harms would be inaccurate. The concept is useful because it forces analysts to identify winners, losers and assumptions.

sections.title: Potential Compensation Is Not Payment
sections.body_md: Kaldor-Hicks reasoning asks whether winners could hypothetically compensate losers and still retain a net gain. It does not mean that they actually do so. The criterion can inform cost-benefit analysis but leaves distribution unresolved. A lawyer should identify whether actual compensation, consent or rights protection is legally required under the policy. Substituting a potential-payment test for enforceable protection can be especially unfair to people with little political power.

sections.title: Values Remain Contestable
sections.body_md: An economic assessment depends on which outcomes are measured and how they are valued. Court access, privacy, dignity and freedom may not fit neatly into a monetary total. A legally legitimate decision must apply the governing rights, powers and procedures even when an economic model favors another result. The useful skill is to state the model's conclusion and its limits in the same paragraph. That keeps evidence in service of law rather than above it.

orange.focus: Evaluate regulatory capture and unequal influence
orange.summary: Advanced policy analysis examines whether institutions charged with protecting the public come to serve the industries they oversee. Identify evidence and incentives without treating every regulatory disagreement as corruption.
checklist: I can define regulatory capture carefully
I can recognize information and revolving-door concerns
I can propose safeguards consistent with due process

sections.title: Regulators Need Information
sections.body_md: A financial regulator may depend on industry expertise to understand complex products. That information can improve rules, but it also creates the risk that regulated parties shape decisions in their own interests. Regulatory capture describes institutional alignment with private interests contrary to the regulator's public mandate. It is not established merely because an agency meets industry representatives. A careful analyst looks for evidence about decisions, incentives, transparency and effects on protected persons.
sections.audio_script: A financial regulator may depend on industry expertise to understand complex products. That information can improve rules, but it also creates the risk that regulated parties shape decisions in their own interests. Regulatory capture describes institutional alignment with private interests contrary to the regulator's public mandate. It is not established merely because an agency meets industry representatives. A careful analyst looks for evidence about decisions, incentives, transparency and effects on protected persons.

sections.title: Concentration Changes Influence
sections.body_md: A few firms with substantial resources may be able to monitor consultations, fund research and lobby officials more effectively than dispersed consumers. This can distort whose evidence enters the rulemaking process. Public notice, conflict disclosure, balanced consultation and independent analysis can reduce some risks, but each has implementation costs. The legal framework determines which procedures are required. An advanced argument separates demonstrable unfair process from speculation about officials' motives.

sections.title: Design for Reviewable Expertise
sections.body_md: A regulator can publish supporting evidence, explain its assumptions, manage conflicts of interest and allow affected persons to contest material findings. Such measures may protect legitimacy without requiring officials to reject useful technical knowledge simply because industry supplied it. The evaluation should ask whether the resulting rules serve the statutory mandate, respect rights and reduce actual harm. The goal is a knowledgeable and accountable institution, not an institution insulated from all contact with the people it regulates.

black.focus: Defend a law-and-economics theory that serves justice
black.summary: At doctoral depth, integrate empirical insight, distributive justice, public law and professional ethics. Develop policy frameworks that measure effects while protecting nonnegotiable rights and client autonomy.
checklist: I can critique efficiency as a sole objective
I can evaluate inequality in willingness-to-pay measures
I can design accountable empirical review of legal policy

sections.title: Efficiency Is a Tool, Not a Sovereign
sections.body_md: A legal system can use economic analysis to understand incentives and reduce avoidable harm without treating aggregate wealth as its ultimate value. Fundamental rights, fair procedure and democratic authority may constrain otherwise efficient choices. A doctoral theory should specify which objectives are economic, which are legal and which require moral judgment. Hiding those distinctions behind mathematical notation reduces rather than improves rigor.

A doctoral theory should specify which objectives are economic, which are legal and which require moral judgment. Hiding those distinctions behind mathematical notation reduces rather than improves rigor.

sections.title: Who Is Missing From the Model?
sections.body_md: People with little income may appear to value safety less in willingness-to-pay data even when they face the greatest danger. Some harms, including family separation, cultural loss or freedom from coercion, resist reliable market valuation. A serious analyst examines distribution, access and measurement assumptions and may use multiple decision criteria. It should neither discard quantitative evidence nor allow it to decide rights issues that the law entrusts to another process.

sections.title: A Humane Policy Evaluation
sections.body_md: Imagine assessing a reform to legal aid. Measure case outcomes, time, costs and error, but also whether people understood their choices and whether vulnerable groups could obtain meaningful representation. Use a credible counterfactual, independent review and disclosure of limitations. Proposed changes must respect professional duties and lawful authority. The aim is not to maximize a dashboard score. It is to use sound evidence to help legal institutions protect lives, dignity and freedom more effectively.
